I have some professional understanding of stun guns and I can tell you now, they are actually quite basic in design. Their major flaws are that some do not provide enough voltage to pass the skin and spasm the muscles, and the probes that pierce the skin are essentially darts with metal cords (limiting their range and making accuracy crucial). If an assailant has a firearm, the muscle spasm can cause them to fire their weapon, potentially harming you or a bystander.

Increasing the current passing beyond the skin can do much more than just a simple muscle spasm. Depending on the region of the body, the path of the current, and many other factors, the effects could be anything between a painful knockout or death. It is incredibly difficult to gauge the impedance of the human body, because it can differ dramatically between people and between circumstances. If a taser provides a 5KV source and your weakest path to ground is 100 K Ohms, you'll have 20mA of current flowing through your body (will cause some spasm, definitely some pain). However, if your skin is wet, your resistance drops to 5K Ohms, and now the 5KV taser is now generating 1 Amp of current through your body. If you look at this chart, you'll notice that 1 amp of current is actually a fuck load and will absolutely wreck your shit.

There are some variants of stun guns that actually shoot a battery slug with two probes, some that can be fired multiple times, and some that can detect current flow and will limit the voltage to maintain non-lethality. However, cost, questionable non-lethality, and the potential threat of guns make them completely unfeasible in a situation that would otherwise require armaments.

As for rubber bullets and tear gas, they are often used during riots. However, they simply don't have the effectiveness of guns to neutralize an armed threat.

Ever heard of a "tommy gun"? It's a Thompson submachine gun, it's the one you see in all the old gangster movies, with the big round drum on the front - the kind of gun they put in violin cases. Thompsons were available for a short time to civilians, but they were exorbitantly expensive, so most of them were sold overseas, to the military, and to law enforcement.

So if they were prohibitively expensive, and civilian sales so poor, how did they end up being so pervasive with Prohibition-era mobsters? Surely some of their bank heist money went to purchasing them, but more often than not, they stole them from police officers.

I use this as an illustration of a larger point - there will always be an arms race between law enforcement and criminal elements. And it is inevitable that whatever is in the hands of the police will eventually be in the hands of the criminals.

I own guns, I like guns, but I wouldn't be opposed to making them slightly more difficult to buy. Some states I think are already leaning too draconian, but some states (like mine), you can get a semi-automatic handgun with no waiting, no license, no training, and only a felony background check. I wouldn't really mind it being at least as hard to get a gun as it is to get a driver's license.

But truthfully, if we want to see any amount of gun control have any sort of efficacy, it has to start with law enforcement. Most patrol officers have never had to fire their weapon. I think that's an excellent reason to remove firearms from patrol officers and replace them with less-than-lethal alternatives. If an unarmed police force sounds nuts, realize this isn't a novel idea. You can argue it wouldn't work here because we have way more guns than other places - but Norway and Iceland are the 10th and 14th heaviest armed countries in the world, and their police don't carry guns. Mostly, we just see it as necessary because we still have visions of wild west sheriffs with badges and six-shooters, and we think that's the only way law enforcement can work. I feel like it might be time to demand our public servants stop playing cowboy.

So, I think your suggestion that law enforcement move to less-than-lethal alternatives is excellent. There will always be special response teams (like SWAT teams) that are needed to deal with specific situations, but there's no reason for most officers to carry a deadly weapon, and all you accomplish by giving them one is ensuring that any would-be criminal will also seek to carry one.

Perhaps the recent media attention of just how many people die unnecessarily at the hands of police will encourage people to question why they need lethal weapons in the first place. We can only hope.
